notes: Default community strings to try first: public, private.
name: SNMP - Enumeration (Getting Started)
description: Walk SNMP with a community string to dump device/system info. Try public/private, then brute-force community strings with onesixtyone.

defense.why_it_works: SNMP v1 and v2c control access using a plaintext community string. Manufacturer default community strings 'public' and 'private' are frequently left unchanged. Walking SNMP can expose system info, running processes, and credentials passed on the command line.
defense.prerequisites: Network access to UDP 161 and a valid community string (often the default 'public').
defense.impact: System details from the SNMP MIB - running processes, network interfaces, installed software, sometimes credentials.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1046 AN1583] Monitor for execution of network enumeration utilities (nmap, netcat, net.exe, ping.exe, tracert.exe) in short succession, particularly when chained with lateral movement tools or system enumeration commands. [AN1584] Sequential ping, arp, or traceroute commands issued from bash scripts or interactive shells to map remote hosts are a strong behavioral indicator.
defense.artifacts: SNMP GET/WALK requests to UDP 161 in network logs; the agent's access log where enabled.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=network dest_port=161 protocol=udp
| stats count dc(dest_ip) as hosts by src_ip, bin(_time, 1m)
| where count>20 OR hosts>10
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where RemotePort == 161
| summarize probes=count(), hosts=dcount(RemoteIP) by LocalIP, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where probes > 20 or hosts > 10
| sort by probes desc
// snmpwalk SNMP community/OID enumeration on UDP 161
defense.prevention:
Upgrade to SNMPv3 which adds authentication and encryption. Change all default community strings. Restrict SNMP access to authorized management hosts at the firewall (UDP 161/162).

[MITRE T1046 M1042] Disable or remove unnecessary services and functionality that expose attack surface. [M1030] Implement network segmentation to limit the set of hosts reachable from any given compromised system. Use firewalls to restrict which source addresses can reach each service port.
defense.misconfiguration: Common introductory misconfigurations: services running as root/SYSTEM unnecessarily, default credentials unchanged, unnecessary services listening on all interfaces, lack of firewall rules exposing services externally, no monitoring or alerting on authentication failures.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service listening on all interfaces with default creds (common in labs/staging):
ss -tlnp | grep LISTEN
# 0.0.0.0:21  (FTP on all interfaces)
# 0.0.0.0:3306 (MySQL on all interfaces - should be 127.0.0.1 only)
# 0.0.0.0:8080 (Tomcat with manager app accessible)

# Running services as root:
ps aux | grep -E '(mysql|apache|nginx|ftp)'
# root  1234  /usr/sbin/mysqld  <-- should run as 'mysql' user
defense.secure_config:
# Bind services to localhost or specific IPs (not 0.0.0.0):
# MySQL: my.cnf -> bind-address = 127.0.0.1
# Apache: Listen 127.0.0.1:80 (if behind a proxy)

# Run services as dedicated low-priv users:
# systemd unit: User=mysql Group=mysql

# Host-based firewall (ufw):
ufw default deny incoming
ufw allow from 10.10.1.0/24 to any port 22  # SSH from mgmt only
ufw allow 443  # HTTPS
ufw enable

# Change all default credentials immediately after installation
# Enable fail2ban for SSH and web services

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, NetFlow / sFlow, Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Check for unusual network connections to/from the source host
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Walks SNMP to dump device and system information:
  snmpwalk   traverse the MIB tree
  -v 2c      SNMP version 2c
  -c public  the community string (try public, then private)
  <ip>       the target
Returns system info, users, running software, and sometimes credentials; append an OID (e.g. 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0) to target one value, and brute-force community strings with onesixtyone.
